words: Today is the 4th of October, 1975, and we're in Orofino. And the interviewer is Kathy Noggle, and the interviewee is Phyllis McCarthy. That's what everybody says. Okay, now, I'm going to put this, I want to make sure I spell it right, it's P-H-Y-L-L-I-S? Right. And it's M-A-C?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: M-C. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Capital A. A. And your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Perkins.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your birth date?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Weip, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, how do I spell that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: W-E-I-P-P-E.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think I've seen that before.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Going towards Pierce and headquarters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not too much, huh? And your phone number in case they wanted to call you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Do you have any nicknames that people call you now or that they did call you when you were younger?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just Phil. Phil?

words: Is that what they call you in the council meetings?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I have lots of people call me that. Mostly men.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I suppose, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That do it. And I have a few lady friends that don't call me anything else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And let's see, I just had your address written down here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: About 72 Northen Avenue. 146 Johnson Avenue. I don't know which one you want.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'll put them both. This is the biggest apartment I've ever been in. I didn't expect it to keep going back.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we can't be empty anyway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, gosh. Let's see, where did you first come in Idaho? You were already born in Idaho, so you were there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My grandparents that you saw over there in that picture are pioneers. They're all pioneers of Clearwater County.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did they come from?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They came from West Virginia. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Pretty loud pencil.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know whether you have a place to ask that or not. But my grandfather was pretty, and my family are well-known here because they had the first telephone office here and operated the first telephone office in Clearwater County. Oh, really? And they owned the first car in Clearwater County, Samson Snyder.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, that was his name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Samson Snyder.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. We don't get down to grandparents, but now that was your mother's or father's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mother's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mother's family. So her maiden name was Snyder. And her first name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bergie. B-E-R-G-I-E.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Gee, it wasn't short for Virginia. It was just that's it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Very odd name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I would expect it to be a nickname.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you ever heard them called?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it S-N-I-D-E-R or Y?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: S-N-Y-D-E-R. OK.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her birth date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's March the 8th, 1897.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was she born? Back in Virginia, I suppose.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, she was born...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, they came here by the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she was born on a ranch in Lehi, down by the old home of theirs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you were both born there? Yeah. And she's living now. You said she's at the care center? Yeah. And what year did your mother and father get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I can't answer that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, about one. Let's see. She was born in 1987.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It is 83, 1897. I thought I figured that up. 1975, take away 1897.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I have as much trouble as... OK, that's 75 plus 3 is 78.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, then she's 80. She's 83 years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: OK, so we've got to add five more years or take off five more years. 1892.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Was when she must have been born. Because that would be eight years plus 75 would make her 83. OK. So let's see. She would have been eight years old in 1900.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, she was about 23 years old when they were married. OK. So... Can you figure that out?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1952? 1915, maybe? I think so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was born in 1918, and there's two children before me, so it has to be before that. I would say about 19... Because I think she had one right away, and then another one right away. There's not much difference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That might be right then, about 1915?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would say 1914. OK.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did she ever work outside the home, or did she stay?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, she worked outside the home, and of course they had this telephone office. Have you seen... Do you know where the courthouse is?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We went by it yesterday.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And of course there's West Gun and Tackle Shop right... When you notice it, that used to be their home, I remember, going there, and that used to be years... That many years ago used to be the telephone office down in that building.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's where they... That was their business.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was their business, and she worked in the telephone office, I know. Now, where she worked, I have never heard her say anything about working out anyplace else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think she probably did, or you just don't know where it was?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't... I think she might have worked babysitting or something like that for other people back then, but I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But this business went on for quite a while, so she worked...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. They used to be telephone operators, the three girls.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She and her sisters? Two sisters. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And that's all I know about it. Of course, I was thinking about my mother. Her mind is as sharp as a tack. And I don't know whether she would be a good interviewer or not. I would say yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, gee, that would... We might be coming back to the area again, and then that would be fun to get, because then we'd have two generations, too. And we might even get your daughter, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And she is... Well, my daughter has had an interesting life, but anyhow, I would say that if you're back, that my mother would make a good interview, a person to interview.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think that's it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Third-year person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, your father's name is what? Jerry.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: J-E-R-Y. Too bad I have this cold in case I have to get up and... Oh, go feel free. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And his birth date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he was 18 years older than she was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, that'll give us a...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you figured out...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 92 minus 18, then. 74, 1874, maybe. And where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was born in Missouri someplace. I can't remember the town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it was your mother's family that were the pioneers out here. Is your father still living? No. When did he die? Just the year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know if you feel as better at that than I am, but I just cannot remember. He's been dead about 10 years. Okay, about 65? I'd have to look on the back of the picture.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did he do? What were the jobs that he had?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, see, he worked for the telephone company.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was your mother's family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: For the telephone company way back when, and that's where she met him. He was working as a lineman or a telephone company.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, but the telephone company wasn't the same company.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that was him. When he came out here from Missouri when he was a young fella, he worked for the telephone company. I can't tell you what the name it is. And then they farmed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He and your mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Grandpa and Grandma owned this big farm up here in the Weeack Country, and they were put on it and eventually bought it and farmed it all their lives.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your mother and father, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's where all our children were born.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see. So that's why it was the same place as where your mother was born, yeah. It was the homestead. And so he was a telephone company lineman and then he worked the ranch. Okay. And was he... Did they do that up to the time that he retired?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, until he passed away. Yeah. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see, how many brothers and sisters do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have two brothers and three sisters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are your brothers' names and ages?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Kerman, approximately 56. Lewis, Wayne, I would say about 50. That's so hard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can't remember those things. The only way I remember my sister's age is I remember she's seven years older than me, so I have to count up like that too. And then you say you have two sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Three sisters. Thelma is approximately 60.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hi, Debbie.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hi, Debbie. Three. I don't know. That's going to take two hours. I don't have two hours.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think we could... We'll just go to work. Now I'm on your sisters. We've got Thelma.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And Elaine. And let's see, what did I tell you on Thelma?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About 60.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, about 60. And Elaine is 58. And then comes me, and then comes Shirley.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Shirley's baby.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And Shirley's the baby underneath the two boys.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she's in her 40s probably.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, what's Wayne?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 50, about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's somewhere, I would say 47, 48. Okay. There's not too much difference between all those children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, they write no Ls.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the way they did in those days. You know. It's like they say, you've come a long way, baby. You can't make up a language.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, let's see, your husband's name. Is it Gerald or is it Jerry?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's J-A-R-R-E-L-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: J-A-R-R-E-L-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: J-A-R-L? Gerald? Gerald. Huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was named after an Army fellow whose last name was Gerald.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, like a buddy of his father's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, a buddy of his father's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what's his birth date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: March the 18th, 1912.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oregon City, Oregon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you two were married where and when?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were married in Lewiston in 1936. Next year we'll be celebrating our 40th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 40th.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is that the correct year?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that should be. Right? That's really something.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 35, 36, 37, I've got it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 40 years. Now, I noticed on the back of his shirt, does he work in electric?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he had a business here for 20 years, right down underneath. Oh. We own this building. And he was a logger, and he worked in the woods, in fact. And it was a whole new life for us. And we decided to take the plunge.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you moved into town? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We owned a home up here. And we were living here when he was working in the poles. He had his own pole truck. And we decided to do it. These people wanted to sell. And my husband started working for him, for the former owners.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Of this downstairs? Of this building. Was it an appliance shop?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes, and in a small town, it's everything. Uh-huh. Parkwares. My husband, you wouldn't believe him. He can do anything. Anybody, anything, anybody wanted to fix, he could almost fix it. They'd bring in sewing machines, vacuum cleaners. And of course, we sold Whirlpool appliances. And years ago, 20 years ago or more, we won the record.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm telling you, we were the record shop. And if we didn't have the biggest record business in the world, we just made money off of records back when they were selling 78s and all over. And all those things, you know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So when did he make the change from logging to this business? About what years?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's still, he's still, you own it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you know, no, he's retired. And of course, the reason we all have these clothes and so on, and you can make $200 a month on your Social Security. And in this day and age, you have to make every bit of money that you can. So he makes $200 a month doing the same old thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see. Yeah, you can earn up to that much and still get Social Security. Yeah. So he works down in the shop.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we still keep our business, I mean, except it's a lot easier now. I still have my desk out here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I noticed that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have to do my same kind of work in the secretarial end of it as I did when we were in business, only it's on a smaller scale. I do my books every three months instead of every month now. And, you know, he has his pets in business. And he was very well liked.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And of course, some people just probably wouldn't let him retire even if he wanted to just quit the whole thing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course, that's probably right. And that's, now, does that answer your questions on land?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I think really well. Let's see now. Now I can remember your daughter's middle name, Ray, but what was her first name? Eleanor.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Like Eleanor in the, Eleanor, what was her name in the story? Pruitt. Eleanor Pruitt.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her last name now is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thomason, T-H-O-M-A-S-O-N.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her birth date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was May the 20th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We were married in 30, 36?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And is she working outside the house or? No. She's got how many children? Two. She has, or those, one of those.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One of those. And she has a girl.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you had one other daughter, but no son? No. And your other daughter's name was?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Janet Carol, if you want to know the name. Sure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her last name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mary Dahl.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: D-A-H-L. And when was she born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was born in 1936.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She was the older?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Older. And see, we were married on March the 6th, and she was born on March the 8th, a year later.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And my mother's birthday is March the 8th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother and my daughter were both the same date, March the 8th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then she passed away what year? Say that was just a ----

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Three years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was 72?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, three years ago, September the 23rd. 24th, September the 24th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Now, what schooling did you complete?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I've only had a high school education, and of course that, as you grow up to realize. And of course that's where I'm trying to help my grandchildren to not make the same. Because I never had a mother that, in those days, I say, and I don't think I'm wrong, your mother, and of course, and especially my mother, was never a mother to me. I think she was just too busy. I was just like that. But anyhow, I think after you've lived your life and seen all the mistakes you make, you could sure try to help somebody. Yeah. And you could sit down and talk to them. Like, I mean, of course that's one of my main goals in life, is to try and help the grandchildren and talk to them as friends. Whether it does any good or not, I think it's up to them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But some children, it'll do some good, and others, it won't do a bit of good. They have to learn their own way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you say your parents didn't encourage you to go on to college. Did you even think about it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we were—oh, I wish I knew how to express myself on this. I started to—yes, we started to—Kidman Business College in Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you? You and your sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My sister and I, my second sister and I were in the same grade. I skipped one grade in school. And she and I were—graduated together from high school, Elaine. And we were both sent up there to Kidman. But I don't remember the circumstances. I don't remember whether we wanted to go. I don't remember anything. All I remember is being so homesick and quitting, and they had a terrible time with us, and we stayed in people's homes, you know, to work our way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you both stay at the same place?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we didn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see why you would be homesick then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, of course, we weren't prepared for any kind of a life like that. And, of course, I think life then is so different than it is now, you know. I think maybe children are more equipped for that stuff nowadays. They're so independent and so grown up. I just don't know why I have them. Maybe my mother would have an entirely different version. But I just don't hardly remember anything about family life when I was young.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever wanted—have you thought about ever going back to school? Would you be interested in it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I—no, I wouldn't now. No. All I want now is a little peace and quiet in my life. I have worked and poured my heart out in this town for so long, and, of course, there's people that argue with me that say I'm not going to be content to goof around. But I say just watch me. I'm so fed up with— I've been—I've had too much is the way I put it. And I've had too much pressures and too much to do. I just want to be peaceful and quiet and do my own thing now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That makes sense. Really, I can—although I might—if I knew you better, I might agree with some of the people that said you wouldn't be satisfied, you know, if you've had all that responsibility. You might get bored more than someone that has just stayed home. Let's see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm still not getting those questions.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, well, yeah, but we'll just talk about some of them. Now, what would you say your skills are? I know your professional skills and that kind of thing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I say that there's not too much that I can't and couldn't accomplish. I—and thank God my husband is along—goes along with me. We went to grow old gracefully with things to do. And, of course, we took up golfing. And, of course, now I'm going to learn to knit. And he—we both are avid bridge players. And I learned before him. And I was a little concerned that he might not learn. And he kind of balked at it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This bridge? Bridge.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he did. And, of course, I admire and love my husband for all those things. Because we don't want to—I know too many people in my own family, they can't do anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Together?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But sit around and do nothing. And, of course, I can't see it that way. And, of course, we'll be playing golf until the day we won't be able to put one foot in front of the other. And, of course, I think it's good exercise. It's good for the mind. And it's absolutely good therapy for people. I've heard it time and time again. And especially with sorrow in your family, when you lose a child, you never get over it. And, of course, you go out there on that golf course, and you—it's a therapy. You don't think about anything else. And, of course, we love to get together with our friends and play bridge. And I started learning to knit last year. Didn't have too much of a chance. And, of course, this year with this Chamber of Commerce, I could spend every bit of my waking time making that Chamber of Commerce.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sure you could.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So I'm going to be handicapped this winter, for the rest of this winter, for trying to take up knitting again. And I sewed. I have sewed from the time I was first married. But there was a—

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Period when you've been, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was a couple of years in there between when we ran this business that I could not sew. I just had too much to do. Now I'm back to it again. Yeah. And, of course, it was the best thing that ever happened to us when we quit that business. We tried to sell our business, and we couldn't. Then after the death of our daughter, we just did not want it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We couldn't stand it. Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We couldn't stand it. And the two of us working in that business together— I take it that you fellows have a way of starting that thing, and we get wrapped up in our lives, and our—

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that's what is—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't want—and then to listen to that? Oh. It's going to be hell. But, anyhow, we could not stand that business. And we tried to sell it and couldn't. And you know that it was the greatest thing in the world. We didn't think that it could ever be possible. We just quit it, plain quit it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sometimes that's really hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had a big quitting business sale, and to look back on it now, we never dreamed that it would work out so great. And I just—neither I nor anyone can get over how great it was that we took that step.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That you finally—yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Finally took that step.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, did you always—let's see, you got the business in the 50s, early 50s. And you worked there ever since. When did you get your Chamber of Commerce? Is it a parted position?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You're elected? Oh, they have to—the Board of Directors have to elect you. They ask you, and then you're elected.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long have you been doing that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, now, that's only for a year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was last January. Of course, this Chamber of— I was in the Progressive Merchants, what we called the Progressive Merchants in town. And when we were in business, I would just continually—what do you want?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you hold my phone for a second? That's okay. You want me to—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, you know, I worked so hard in that Progressive Merchants. Nobody knows.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that, I suppose, was a paying job. Oh, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was all. But, see, we sure—we had a president. But any time there was anything to do, it was—I was—I spearheaded it. I mean, in fact, I know, and people say that I was president and secretary of both. I was secretary and treasurer, and we had a president. But anyhow, there's a lot of work to it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's a lot of work to it. As much as you'll accept, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we had all these promotions a year that had to be lined out and all that stuff. And then— With any glory to myself, I say it's the state of fact. And anybody in this town that knows me, which a lot do, or is going to tell you the same thing, I tell it like it is. And I just am not—I just cannot be a two-faced person. And if I—and I'll practically tell you out of your face. It's what I think, and I don't know. They say, and I think that most people admire me for that. But OK, the hospital auxiliary, and I'm sure you know what that is, the ladies' bench working for the hospital. And that hospital auxiliary was about to fold. It was in bad shape. They couldn't get anybody to come to the meetings, and they wasn't anything to do with that. And I started it. I joined it about two years—now let's see, this is stuff. Let's see how long I was hospital auxiliary president last year. And I joined it about two years before that. I see. Well, after the death of our daughter, well, your mind starts working a little bit, and I don't know. I just got closer to the hospital. I don't know what it is. But anyhow, I—they—I don't know. I guess they asked me if I would take presidency.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Of the auxiliary?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of the auxiliary. And you know that it amounts to the fact that I put that thing on its feet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm not surprised seeing the other kind of things that you did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I tell you, you just wouldn't believe it. And of course, I got all kinds of compliments and everything. But that does not bother me one bit. I mean, I'm not—my head is not swelled. I don't—it doesn't make one bit of difference whether people say good or bad things about me. It doesn't change me one bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, all three of these things, the Chamber of Commerce and the Emergency Association, the auxiliary, none of them were jobs you got paid for.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no. No. And I—you just can't believe what that hospital auxiliary is doing. Of course, you'd have—you'd have— If they thought I was good, you should know the last year's president, the one that came after me, she was ten times better than I was. And I was good because I believe in doing something. And I believe in publicity and trying to get committees and making them work and everything, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Then I'd say, would you agree that one of your skills, and I mean, this is— Leadership. Yeah, leadership and organization.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And leadership. I've always been a leader. And, of course, you get kind of buff. Well. As my son-in-law tells me, I would make a good first sergeant in the Army. And, of course, his favorite hobby was his bad kid's juice, and that's it. It was dying on the vine. And I don't know what it is about me. I don't know whether people like to be—I think one thing is people like to be told and bought.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, people like to have things clear. They like to have a leader that cracks the whip.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I honestly believe that because I'm telling you, you wouldn't believe the fantastic response and the crowds we're getting. We've had all the way from our lowest meeting has been about 23, 23 people. And we were lucky if we were getting about five or six, as up to 10, 15, 20 in the last two or three years. Now, I was treasurer. I was treasurer of the Chamber of Commerce for 10 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, but it isn't too much of a job. Of course, it takes some more of your time on top of all this other—the business I had to run and all this other stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you've done a lot of bookkeeping work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You have bookkeeping skills, too. Every time I was in an organization, I always ended up being secretary trade. And you know, it just follows from people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I think so. What other skills would you list, then? Not hobbies, not crafts and things, but you have leadership skills and bookkeeping. What other skills would you say that you've used in what work you've done?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What would you say, Kathy, from concentrating?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think that leadership—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think you should clean houses. Yeah. I mean, and a clean place. Our building has to look just right. And I still say that. That's the clean and painted and all. It was all just nice. But I still say that that is where you get some of your looking up to and attention, because most people like that. You take a building that's run down and kept inside and out, not well kept.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have something to do with this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is this the one that cost the feet?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The one they chipped away the brick?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's nice of you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I've been hollering ever since, waving these flags, because I think it's a fantastic thing for our thing. And I honored it in the chamber. Oh, really? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because I know you spoke last night about beautification, and you're interested in it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And of course, I talk about that all the time, because any person that likes to keep neat children, neat houses, neat businesses, neat streets and everything is bound to want something like that for your town. Yeah. If I could crack the whip and tell everybody in this that has a business here to shape up and fix their buildings up and clean them up and everything, that's what I could do. That's what I do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever gotten any awards or honors for either any of the organizations you've been in or any of the work you've done, or for any crafts or anything? Have you ever gotten any recognition?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, except they had me up as woman of the year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that's something.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I lost. I mean, I didn't get it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were nominated.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was nominated.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that last year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Year before last.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever entered anything in a fair?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No, I've never had time for that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Well, now if I can get to some more general questions. You already know some of the things I wanted to ask. What can you say? What comes to mind in describing the difference between a rural woman and an urban woman? You've lived here since before you got married. Do you consider yourself, do you consider it rural or urban?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I consider it rural. Now, I think your first question, what can you tell the difference between an urban and a rural woman? Well, you can't. Some women, I mean, maybe their lives are different. You can't tell whether that's some old farmer woman or some old urban woman. And by that, though, it has to do with the difference in their lives. Actually, I can't tell. Now, what are we talking about? Well, sure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What would you say? Which is more appealing to you? What do you think the advantages are to being a rural over urban woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's like everything has its advantages and disadvantages. But of course, as I told you before, I would always be partial and say more advantages to a rural community and their life. And possibly because that's been my life. And I can't stand a large town. I think people are too unfriendly. Although in a small town, most everybody knows about your business, too. But I don't care. And naturally, you're going to have a lot more advantages in a large town than there's in a community.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, what kind of advantages are you talking about in a large town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you can see and go to 10 times more in the arts and entertainment. What shall we call it? Shall we call it from the very low class to the high class?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that makes sense.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And of course, I don't know. Just more things to see. Just take this community compared with Spokane. Even that. And of course, there's 10 times more crime. And I think the drug problem is 10 times easier to control in a small town than it is in a large town, too. I still think it's fine if everybody knows, supposedly knows, about everybody else's business. I still think you can have a better life and identify and communicate more with another person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In a small town? Yeah, I think that makes sense.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd like to hear your opinion.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, of course, I listen to so many different people that I was thinking of something I was going to ask you, though. Now, I think you'd agree you're a strong enough woman that sat down in any place, you wouldn't wither away. But take a kind of a timid woman who's, oh, I don't know what to say, except who grew up very traditionally and whose mother always stayed in the home. Do you think that woman would have more of a chance of doing something with her life or of doing...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In a small place or in a large city?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would say in a large city.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think she'd be more likely to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I do. I wouldn't think like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And why?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I might be wrong. Well, because, maybe it's because I think a small town is too cruel. You take that timid person, that... I think you're speaking about a timid person that doesn't do too much. You know, I'm not a timid person, you know. And as you say, I'm a very strong person when it comes to... And a leader, okay, you take this other kind of a person. And yet on the other hand, that might be hard to answer. In a small town, maybe somebody could take her by the hand and pour into a person like me or make her feel better or whatever. Whereas maybe in a large town, she would just be lost in the crowd. I don't know, but it seems to me like she would be more apt to do something with herself in a large town. Now that's all I can comment on that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm interested in that. In fact, it's the first time it's come up as a question, and I'd like to see what some other people say about it. I tend to agree with you. You were saying back when we were talking about things, your brothers and sisters and your mother, that you can't remember that much about your family life when you were younger.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Can I say one thing?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That what I wanted to ask was, are there any comparisons you can make between your family life now with you being the mother and with your grown daughter and your grandchildren and the family life back when your mother was the mother and you and your sisters and brothers were the young children. Are there any similarities left or do you think it's all the times have changed all that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Kathy, of course, I'm going to get to all these worries you see about life. It's why I can't remember. I don't know why I can't remember. And I had a history actually when I was very young. And they say, I have heard and I have thought that they say that that'll cause you to have a bad memory. I don't know whether my mind has been filled with so much stuff that I don't have time to do it, whether you have to train me more, whether I have to have another education. But it has always worried me. My memory is bad, bad. And I cannot, I just cannot remember. The other sisters and some of the people talking to me, it's just completely blank. I mean, I just don't want to remember. Do you remember a lot about your childhood?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I do. I remember more than a lot of people, I think. I can go back way far. Maybe a couple years when I can't remember, when we were moving a lot. But all the time we stayed in one place. But I heard this enough times from other people about their memories that, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It worries me. Does it? Yeah. Really? Does it, I mean, do you hear it from other people?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, a lot, a lot. And especially some people, you know, some will say they can remember things way far back but they can't remember things last week and some will say the opposite. But you do say you remember your mother was really busy when your kids were little.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think she was terribly busy. I probably don't remember if she were having cows and chickens and gardens and having children all the time. I imagine she was too. A lot of bad times.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think you spent more time with your kids than she was able to spend? That was probably pretty busy times for you too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, of course we had more time. You know, she was, I would say, my life, when I was in there, there was nothing whatever compared to her life. I only had two children and a whole different life.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This is another thing that we have run into. It's fairly predictable, but many women, or most of the women that came from larger families had smaller families. Do you think it had to do, do you think it's just a function of birth control that's available or do you think that, for instance, did you make a conscious decision and say, I remember I had a lot of brothers and sisters around, I don't want that many people in my family so we'll just have two or...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't exactly remember. I don't know. I know that I didn't have many children, so I suppose that's, a lot of children, so I suppose that's the answer to it. My mother told me that they just didn't know any better. You know, Kathy, the times are so different. I mean, they're really, and God knows what it's going to be like in the next generation, but back in my mother's generation to my generation, it was so different, take from my generation to these grandchildren's generation, it is so different.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she tell you about, did you find out about children and bearing children and where they come from from your mother? Did you? Just something, when you had one you found out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know if I did what I did because...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They didn't discuss it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And of course if my mother, if you'd asked her, maybe she'd tell you, but I remember nothing about her ever talking to me, and I don't think she did. I don't think she did any of the chores. If she was a, I don't know if all mothers are like my mother or not, but I think that she never, that her children just didn't mean much to her. They were there and that was it. That's the impression that I have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's interesting. I wonder if that has to do with generations too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. I don't have a very close relationship with my mother, never did, and I never will, and I don't know if there's any other families that have that same feeling or not. I'm not that close. Maybe I'm too, maybe I should say things that aren't true, but I usually don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, how about when your daughters came of age, did you sit down with them and talk to them about childbirth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think I did my own daughters, but I'm telling you it's different with big granddaughters. Of course, I presume that there's a lot to do with their mother not being here, and maybe it's because I'm older and wiser and have learned, and I would say that so much varies. A lot has to do with it, with their mother being gone. I just wish that everybody could talk to their children and Mike, I'm talking to these grandkids because I think that it would be, I mean, I'm telling them that I'm their friend, as one of their grandmothers, and that I care, and yet I'll listen to them. In other words, I think I'm the greatest mother in the world now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I know what you mean.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But unfortunately, everybody can't, it's too bad everybody can't become a grandmother before they're older.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before they're, yeah. Let's see, I want to check back here. You were married in 36, and you were how old then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was, let's see, when did this take place? I was 13 years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So is that, did you get married fairly soon after you came back from Spokane, after you quit business school? No, I didn't. What, did you know your husband before you'd left?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, no, no. I'm not going into that either. I don't have an ideal romance and all that stuff. But, you know, sometimes we don't, we sure don't interview people about that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, no, we just, well, like I say, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In other words, you might like to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sure, these are the kind of, some of the things that would be interesting, or that we have asked of, you know, why did you decide to get married.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My interview belongs in a true story, not in a gossipy one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you'd rather not talk about that particular, OK. Well, let me ask, you've kind of explained what you do for recreation. Tell me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like you've got some things that you and your husband do together, like the bridge and golf, and then some things that you do on your own, knitting and sewing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you wouldn't expect him to do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know, but it sounds like you've got a mixture there, that you don't have to do all your things together, but that you do some things together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We go a lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You go sightseeing, traveling?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Vacationing, yeah, and going away. And, but we'll never do a lot of, now, I'm just foolish enough to think that I came to the province, or we'd have probably been known to be that tight for many years. And of course, my husband began to think, of course, they were trying to run me for another year, and they'd probably run me from now on, too, really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If you'd take it. If you'd take it, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because it's, I can see where it means somebody retired. I don't know how many of these people do what I did this year, rather than this year, and in a small town, that's what you're going to find.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because it takes all your heart and energy to run your business. And anyhow, he told me that he would divorce me if I was coming again, because we want to travel. And I think that when death hits close to you like this, I think it changes your view about life.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Makes life a little more precious.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You bet you want to live for today.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Then you think that's had a big effect on your attitude about what you want out of your life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think you get awful independent, too. And I've talked with others that feel the same way. So I don't think I'm alone in it. You know, you just feel like you're here today and gone tomorrow. So you just live your life a lot different. You sort of live it with a passion.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I think I can understand that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that personally, I think that, and I don't know, maybe that's what makes you keep your sanity. And it would have been so much better if we had got a, if we still had a stepmother, but you've heard of a typical mean stepmother. Yeah. Well, we have one. And of course, that makes it a lot harder.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I think he remarried.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he remarried within eight months to a witch. And she hated me. She hated me for the time being, because I stand for too much, I think. And she was just insanely jealous of the memory, I suppose. It's terrible. It's been three years now, and she can't, and it's never got any better. But anyhow, you just, when you have those things to live with, it's hard. And you live with your, and I don't know, I thought I was pretty big, but I don't think I've tried, and I don't think I'm big enough to go down there now and tell her let's forget the past and then. I just don't think I can do it. She's done too much to these children and to me and to the family and everything else. And I said, I tried two years ago, we did, and it didn't work out. So I don't think I'm big enough to do it anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I think I see what you mean.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, you don't. Nobody knows until they've been in it themselves.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, let me ask you this. This isn't, it isn't on the subject, but in your life now, you lived through the Depression and through World War II. What, of those two, which affected you the most? Which did you think was a, oh, which was a bigger disaster in your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can't answer that at all because I don't remember nothing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't remember any depression. I don't remember war. I don't know of anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, let's see, the Depression you would have been about, I forgot. You were 18 and you got married in 36, so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What was the Depression?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The Depression right in, say 1930, say 29, 30. That was about six, you were about 12, so you were pretty small.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But see, my mother, I remember my mother saying now that the Depression didn't affect us too bad. We had a farm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think it was because you were out here, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sure, and that farm was our, I suppose, we didn't go hungry, and I suppose we didn't have too many clothes, but I don't know. I don't remember one thing about that, and I should have been old enough to remember that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know, I think that's pretty young. You know, you were only in fifth or sixth grade or something. Now, World War II, that would have been about 10 years before you got this business, so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When was World War II?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 45, well, 43 through 45. I don't remember that at all. After you were married, did Jerry have to go on the service, or was he already done?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he never was in the service, and I can't answer that. Oh, I had a brother that was in the service, Wayne, and I, but he never. I don't know. I don't know, too. I guess it's probably over two.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're doing a fine job. I mean, you're really being articulate.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think you just. . . Honestly, it's not as if it's got to, but I. . . I like your words, and of course, you can do that yourself, but my mind is my system, and I haven't. You can self-train yourself. Yeah. Train yourself. You can read, and you can self-educate yourself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I haven't. I don't want to put words in your mouth, but I think the fact that you've been appointed and elected to the kind of positions that you have speaks highly. Yeah, I don't. . . You don't think they would ask somebody to do that that they thought couldn't express themselves.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, if I get called up in a meeting or something, and I just the other night, we had a meeting on the 1st of October, and oh, my goodness, I had to know Robert's rules and orders.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I remember that kind of stuff. And I didn't remember it. Well, I didn't say I remember that problem.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I said, I said, I know, I know that I don't know how to go through this meeting just all efficiency-like. I said, I need help, and so I just asked somebody, and of course, they get the big bang out of it, and they don't care. So what? So? I'm too old to care about it anymore. I don't care about that stuff anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you're still willing to learn. I mean, if you don't know and you ask, that's learning, too. It doesn't mean you have to go to school. We haven't talked about anything about religion. Do you go to church or do you consider yourself religious, or does it occupy a very big place in your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, come to, if you sit down and analyze yourself, me, and think about this, I am absolutely no good. I support the church with a check. I'm a Methodist with faith.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I do not go to church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I don't want to go to church.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I feel like it's just like anything else. The church needs help just like the Chamber of Commerce. I should turn it the other way around. The hospital on Zillow needs help just like the church. And so I don't want to help in the church. So I'm helping this other way. I don't know what's wrong with me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm not an atheist.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, of course, I knew this ministry, the administration would change ministries, and I knew this other one real, real well. And I came right out and I told them the very same thing I'm telling you. And if they dislike me for it, that's their business. But I am not going to church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it, was there a time in your life earlier when you were more, when you went to church more often?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was, I was, just like my husband, he was a saint. He was made to go to church. It was one of his earlier lives. And he was, he was a saint.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that somebody to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You're an amazing man. And, of course, I don't know whether you're kidding me or something, but I don't think so. My guess is that you don't have to go to church to be a good person. And maybe that's the wrong attitude, but that's both my husband's attitude. And we had religion forced down us when we were little. And it just didn't, I mean, it just didn't seem real. And I don't know that, but we're very strong supporters financially. We're always tied. And so that's that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: OK, let's see. I just got, there are a couple more things that I want to get your views on. What suggestions would you give a woman who is moving to a rural area who hadn't lived there before?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I mean, try to explain that a little more.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, what would, what, If you knew of someone that wasn't used to a rural area and said, I'm afraid to move there, I don't know what it'll be like, I don't know how to go about making friends or whatever.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course, I don't have any sympathy for those kind of people at all. Because I guess it's because I'm not that kind of a person. And I can't, you can do anything if you want to. And I suppose I, if I were to help him or anything, I'd probably baby him along for a while. And then I'd probably tell him right out to pitch in and start helping him. And shape up. Because, what is there to tell him?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's, that's,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can't answer that anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a fair thing to say. What, let me get a couple of names of magazines from you. What kind of magazines do you subscribe to? You and your husband alone, I mean together, or are you alone? What do you enjoy reading?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Kathy, we, you can believe it or not, now that's one thing that we're looking forward to. I, I don't know how my life's going to come out, but I want to live for myself for the two of us. And we take the readers by joy, and that is all. Oh, he takes the popular mechanics, and he loves that, and we read the readers by joy. And then he's, now that is all. And I am not very intellectual.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about TV programs, do you enjoy? Are there some that are really your favorite? Do you watch it much? I know you're pretty busy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we watch lots in the evening. Well, yeah, I like a lot of shows. Well, you want me to?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind? Do you like musical entertainment, or there's lots of police shows on?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I, we like Cher, and we like, oh dear, what's the two shows, we always watch Cannon, and Kojak, and we like good music, movies, and no, we like some with a story to it. And especially I like love stories. And I don't, I do not like musical comedy. In fact, I've about summed myself up that I'm not a very happy person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you have not.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't like to read the comedy, and I can't stand any of those

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Situation comedy shows like that,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hogan's Heroes, and I just can't stand anything that's lighthearted. So you can figure out what kind of a person I am.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're too hard on yourself.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Too serious, that's what it is. Now, anything else?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I got one last thing for you, and this is, I'm just going to leave it up to you. Is there anything else that you'd like to say as a rural woman? About your life or about, or about being a woman and living in a rural community or? Well, I should mention that you're about to come to the conclusion

speaker: Speaker 2
words: that I'm not a woman, I'm a man. That'll be a good thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're saying at least you're not a woman in the traditional housewife sense, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And yet I think I'm a beautiful person when it comes to the housekeeping. I love to cook, I love to clean, I love to wash, all those things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But would you be happy just doing that? Yes. Would you? Now, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I'm looking forward to our new home, and I just love to do those things. And I also communicate a lot better with a man than a woman.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That sounds like Sarah last night, part of her story, that she thought. If you remember, that was the last one I did. And she says at first because she sounded like a man or liked to do things that men liked that she thought she had more in common with them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, men just like me better than women, and I just like men better than women. I just don't know. And of course I'm like, as which one of the women said, I like me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was Sarah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: First you have to like yourself. But sometimes I hate myself, but that's natural. I get so mad. I have, to me, I have everything in the world a person could want. And why are you unhappy? Why does life make you feel that way, unhappy? And yet, that's the truth, and that's what shakes me up every time I get down in the dumps. I have everything in the world a person could want.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think that's a beautiful place to end it. I really do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that is. And I tell you, I have the finest husband in the world. And no problems with the children, unhealthy children. There's been nothing like that that I've ever had. No don't want for anything, have enough money to don't want. Now what more could a person want?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know. But I guess there are things, though, that you still want to do. You're building a house, is that it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I want to build a house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you want to travel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And another thing, Kathy, that you can't imagine until it happens to you, my husband shot a man and robbed an art store.

speaker: Speaker 1
